paragraphs.paraphrase: Eurycleia, an old servant, hurries upstairs laughing, suddenly nimble with joy, to wake her mistress Penelope. Leaning over her as she sleeps, she tells her that her husband Odysseus has truly come home at last and has killed the suitors who had been living off his property and mistreating his son.

barriers.quote: my dear child
barriers.my_reading: Eurycleia is an old household servant (Penelope calls her 'nurse' in the next paragraph) who speaks with the affection of a former nanny. Because she calls Penelope 'my dear child', it reads as if she raised Penelope; the text never says whose nurse she was.
barriers.note: Outside knowledge only: she was Odysseus's childhood nurse. Nothing in Book 23 says so.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Penelope tells Eurycleia the gods must have driven her mad, since she used to be sensible. She scolds her for mocking her with nonsense and for waking her from the best sleep she has had since Odysseus left for 'that city'. She sends her back to the women's rooms, saying only her age saves her from a harsh telling-off.

barriers.quote: My good nurse
barriers.my_reading: 'Nurse' in the old sense of a nanny who brought up a child in the family, not a medical nurse.

barriers.quote: that city with its ill-omened name
barriers.my_reading: Troy, the city Odysseus went off to (to war). She won't say its name because it has brought only misfortune.
barriers.note: Troy is never named anywhere in Book 23; outside knowledge only.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Eurycleia insists she isn't mocking her: Odysseus really is back. He was the stranger everyone kept mistreating in the hall. His son Telemachus knew all along and kept the secret so they could take revenge on the suitors.

barriers.quote: in the gallery
barriers.my_reading: The great hall where the suitors feasted and where the killing happened, not a balcony, corridor or art gallery.
barriers.note: Recurs in ¶8 and ¶24; only the fire and pillars mentioned in ¶8 show it is the main hall.

barriers.quote: He was the stranger
barriers.my_reading: Odysseus had been in the house disguised as an unknown visitor (later: dirt and shabby clothes), and the suitors abused him without knowing who he was.
barriers.note: The disguise is taken for granted, not explained, in this Book.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Penelope jumps out of bed, hugs Eurycleia and cries with joy, then asks how Odysseus could possibly have overcome so many suitors on his own.

Eurycleia says she didn't see the fight: she and the other women hid huddled in their shut room, hearing the suitors groan as they died, until Telemachus fetched her on his father's orders. She found Odysseus standing among heaps of bodies, spattered with blood and filth like a lion, a sight she says Penelope would have enjoyed. The bodies are now piled in the gatehouse of the outer courtyard, Odysseus is purifying the house by burning sulfur, and he has sent for Penelope so they can finally be happy together.

barriers.quote: purify the house with sulfur
barriers.my_reading: Burning sulfur to fumigate the hall, cleansing it of the stench and the pollution of the killing (partly practical, partly religious).

paragraphs.paraphrase: Penelope tells her not to celebrate too soon. Everyone, she and her son most of all, would love Odysseus to return, but the story can't be true: some god, angry at the suitors' arrogance toward everyone, rich or poor, must have destroyed them. Odysseus himself, she insists, died far from his homeland and will never come back.

barriers.quote: the Achaean land
barriers.my_reading: Greece, the Greek homeland; 'Achaeans' seems to mean the Greeks.
barriers.note: Never explained; recurs in ¶27. Outside knowledge only.

barriers.quote: It is some god who is angry with the suitors
barriers.my_reading: She accepts that the suitors are dead but insists a god killed them, not Odysseus. The swing from tears of joy (¶3) to flat denial is abrupt and unexplained.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Eurycleia protests that Penelope has always been slow to believe; Odysseus is sitting by his own fire at this moment. As further proof, she saw his old boar-wound scar while washing him and wanted to tell Penelope, but he cleverly clapped his hands over her mouth. She stakes her life on it: if she is lying, Penelope may have her put to the cruelest death.

barriers.quote: the scar the wild boar gave him
barriers.my_reading: An old scar from a boar attack, a known identifying mark. The washing scene and the story of the scar are referred to as if already known; Book 24 later says it came from a boar's tusk on a hunt.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Penelope replies that, however wise the nurse is, nobody can understand the gods' plans. Still, she will go down to her son so she can see the dead suitors and the man who killed them.

barriers.quote: you can hardly fathom the counsels of the gods
barriers.my_reading: 'Counsels' = plans. She means the gods' doings are beyond human understanding, implying the scar proves nothing (a god may be behind it all). The link between this remark and the nurse's evidence is left unstated; note she still says 'the man who has killed them', not 'my husband'.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Penelope comes downstairs, torn between keeping her distance to question him and going straight to embrace him. Crossing the hall, she sits by the fire facing Odysseus, who sits by a pillar looking at the ground, waiting for her to speak. She stays silent a long time, stunned: one moment she looks him full in the face, the next his ragged clothes stop her recognizing him, until Telemachus rebukes her.

barriers.quote: against the wall at right angles to the one by which she had entered
barriers.my_reading: She sat against a side wall, perpendicular to the wall with the door she came in by, across the fire from him.
barriers.note: Hard to picture and adds little; sounds odd aloud.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Telemachus scolds his mother, so hard-hearted he can hardly call her 'Mother', for keeping away from his father instead of sitting beside him and asking him questions. No other wife, he says, could hold back from a husband home after twenty years of suffering; her heart has always been stone.

Penelope tells Telemachus she is too astonished to speak, to ask or answer questions, or even to look the man in the face. But if he really is Odysseus, the two of them will soon know each other, because they share secret signs no one else knows.

barriers.quote: tokens with which we two are alone acquainted
barriers.my_reading: Secret signs or tests that only the two of them know about.
barriers.note: Old-fashioned phrasing; awkward aloud.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus smiles and tells Telemachus to let his mother test him however she likes; she is rejecting him only because he is dirty and in rags. The more urgent question is what to do next: normally a man who kills even one person with few relatives to avenge him must flee the country, and they have killed the leading young men of the whole town, so Telemachus should think about it.

barriers.quote: presently
barriers.my_reading: 'Soon', not 'at present'.
barriers.note: Archaic sense; recurs in Book 24.

barriers.quote: even if the dead man would leave few friends to take up his quarrel
barriers.my_reading: 'Even if hardly anyone would seek revenge for the victim.' The unstated conclusion: if one killing forces exile, killing the town's leading men is far more dangerous.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Telemachus answers that his father should decide, since people say he is the wisest man alive, and promises that he and the others will follow him willingly and not fail him while their strength lasts.

barriers.quote: Look to it yourself, father
barriers.my_reading: 'You work it out, father' / 'that's for you to decide'.
barriers.note: Archaic.

barriers.quote: you will not find us fail you
barriers.my_reading: 'We won't let you down.'
barriers.note: Odd grammar; sounds wrong aloud.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus's plan: they should wash and put on clean clothes, the maids should go and dress up, and the singer Phemius should play dance music on his lyre, so anyone passing will think a wedding is being celebrated. That way news of the suitors' deaths won't spread through town before they can slip away to the woods on Odysseus's own land, where they'll decide what the gods allow them to do next.

barriers.quote: First wash and put your shirts on
barriers.my_reading: Wash off the blood and put on clean tunics or clothes.
barriers.note: 'Put your shirts on' sounds as if they were bare-chested; unclear why.

paragraphs.paraphrase: They do exactly that: they wash and dress, the women get ready, and Phemius strikes up music that makes everyone want to sing and dance. The house rings with dancing, and people outside conclude the queen has finally remarried, criticizing her for not holding out and guarding her husband's property until he returned.

The townspeople don't know what has really happened. Inside, the housekeeper Eurynome bathes Odysseus, rubs him with oil and dresses him in a tunic and cloak, and Athena makes him look taller and stronger, with thick curling hair, giving him a glow the way a master craftsman gilds silver. Looking like a god, he sits down again opposite Penelope, reproaches her for having the hardest heart of any woman (repeating Telemachus's words), and tells the nurse to make up a bed so he can sleep alone.

barriers.quote: The upper servant Eurynome
barriers.my_reading: A senior household servant (housekeeper), a different woman from the nurse Eurycleia.
barriers.note: The two names sound almost the same, especially aloud; only ¶24 ('Eurynome and the nurse') shows they are two people.

barriers.quote: anointed
barriers.my_reading: Rubbed his skin with oil after the bath, ordinary grooming rather than a religious ceremony.

barriers.quote: flow down in curls like hyacinth blossoms
barriers.my_reading: His hair hung in thick, clustered curls, like the tightly packed curly florets of a hyacinth (perhaps dark in color too).

barriers.quote: as a skillful workman enriches a piece of silver plate by gilding it
barriers.my_reading: Athena made his head and shoulders shine with grace, just as a master craftsman makes a silver object more splendid by overlaying it with gold.
barriers.note: 'Silver plate' could be pictured as a dinner plate.

barriers.quote: a man who has studied every kind of art under Hephaestus or Athena
barriers.my_reading: Describes the craftsman in the comparison, not Odysseus; 'his work' also means the craftsman's. Hephaestus is presumably a god of craftsmanship, but the text never says so.
barriers.note: Long inserted clause, hard to follow aloud. Hephaestus identified by outside knowledge only (smith god).

barriers.quote: No other woman could bear to keep away from her husband
barriers.my_reading: Odysseus repeats Telemachus's rebuke from ¶9 word for word. It reads either as a deliberate echo or as an accidental duplication.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Penelope answers that she means neither to be haughty nor to slight him, but his appearance doesn't sweep her off her feet, since she remembers well what he was like when he sailed from Ithaca. Then she tells Eurycleia to move out the bed Odysseus himself built and make it up for him with fleeces, coverlets and blankets.

barriers.quote: I am not struck by your appearance, for I very well remember what kind of a man you were
barriers.my_reading: Ambiguous: either 'your fine new looks don't sway me, because I remember the real Odysseus' (still doubting) or 'I'm not amazed, because I know exactly what you were like' (half-recognizing him). She seems deliberately noncommittal.

barriers.quote: Bring the bed outside this room
barriers.my_reading: Move the bed out of the bedroom Odysseus built and set it up somewhere else. 'This room' is confusing because she is speaking in the hall, not in the bedroom.

paragraphs.paraphrase: This is a test, and Odysseus flares up: who has moved his bed? No man could do it without a god's help, because he built it himself around a living olive tree. He built the bedroom walls and roof around the trunk, cut off the top, shaped the trunk into the bed's post, drilled it, inlaid the bed with gold and silver and stretched crimson leather across it. He demands to know whether it is still in place or someone has cut the olive at its roots.

barriers.quote: She said this to try him
barriers.my_reading: 'Try' = test. Her order was a trap: she knew the bed can't be moved, and only the real Odysseus would know why.
barriers.note: The key point of the scene hangs on this one old-fashioned verb.

barriers.quote: made the trunk the center post of my bed
barriers.my_reading: The rooted olive trunk, trimmed and smoothed, forms one fixed post of the bed, so the bed is anchored to the living tree and can't be moved without cutting it down.

barriers.quote: I then bored a hole down the middle
barriers.my_reading: Unclear: perhaps he drilled holes in the trunk to fit the rest of the bed frame. 'Down the middle' of what is not said.

barriers.quote: making it straight by drawing a line on the wood
barriers.my_reading: He marked a straight guideline on the trunk and trimmed it to that line.

barriers.quote: I stretched a hide of crimson leather from one side of it to the other
barriers.my_reading: Red leather (straps or a whole hide) stretched across the frame as the base that holds the bedding.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Hearing this proof, Penelope breaks down, runs weeping to him, throws her arms round his neck and kisses him. She begs him not to be angry: the gods denied them a life together, and she held back only for fear of being fooled by an impostor. She cites Helen, who would never have gone off with a foreigner had she known the Greeks would come to fetch her back, a wrong that caused all their sorrows. Now that he has described their bed, which only the two of them and one maid (Actor's daughter, who guards their door) have ever seen, she believes him.

barriers.quote: Zeus’s daughter Helen would never have yielded herself to a man from a foreign country
barriers.my_reading: Helen (of Troy) ran off with a foreign man, and the Greeks' war to bring her back caused all their sorrows, including Odysseus's absence. Penelope seems to cite her as a warning of what trusting the wrong man can lead to, to justify her caution, but the link is left implicit.
barriers.note: Paris, Troy and the war are not named; outside knowledge only. 'Zeus's daughter' is also unexplained.

barriers.quote: the daughter of Actor
barriers.my_reading: A maid whose father was a man named Actor (a personal name, not the profession). She came with Penelope from her father's house when she married and guards the bedroom door.
barriers.note: Heard aloud it sounds like 'the daughter of an actor'.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Now Odysseus weeps too as he holds his faithful wife. She is as glad of him as shipwrecked men, swimming after a storm from Poseidon has smashed their ship, are glad to reach land (the few who make it, crusted with salt), and she can't take her arms from his neck. They would have wept until dawn, but Athena lengthened the night, holding back the Dawn goddess at the ocean's edge and not letting her harness her two horses, Lampus and Phaethon, to bring the day.

barriers.quote: As the sight of land is welcome to men who are swimming toward the shore
barriers.my_reading: The long simile starts from Odysseus's tears but describes Penelope's feelings: she is the exhausted survivor and he is the land. The switch of viewpoint mid-sentence is easy to miss.
barriers.note: Long simile with an inserted dash clause; hard to follow aloud.

barriers.quote: indulging their sorrow
barriers.my_reading: Weeping together over everything they had suffered: tears of release, not unhappiness at the reunion.

barriers.quote: rosy-fingered Dawn
barriers.my_reading: Dawn pictured as a goddess whose fingers are the pink streaks of first light.

barriers.quote: held night back in the far west, while she would not allow Dawn to leave Oceanus
barriers.my_reading: Athena miraculously lengthened the night: she kept night from ending and held the Dawn goddess back in Oceanus (apparently the ocean at the edge of the world where day begins), so Dawn could not harness her horses Lampus and Phaethon.
barriers.note: Oceanus is never explained; outside knowledge only.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Eventually Odysseus tells Penelope their troubles aren't over: a long, hard ordeal of unknown length still lies ahead of him, as the ghost of Tiresias foretold when Odysseus went down to the land of the dead to ask about his own and his companions' homecoming. For now, though, he suggests they go to bed and sleep.

barriers.quote: the shade of Tiresias
barriers.my_reading: 'Shade' = ghost. Tiresias is a dead prophet (called 'the Theban prophet' in ¶26), and 'Hades' is the land of the dead.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Penelope says he can go to bed whenever he likes now that the gods have brought him home, but since he has raised the subject he should tell her about this ordeal now; she would have to hear it eventually, so better at once.

Reluctantly Odysseus explains. Tiresias told him to travel carrying an oar until he reaches people who know nothing of the sea, ships or oars and don't even salt their food. The sign will be a traveler asking whether he is carrying a winnowing shovel; there he must plant the oar in the ground and sacrifice a ram, a bull and a boar to Poseidon, then go home and sacrifice to all the gods in turn. His own death will come 'from the sea', gently, in a peaceful old age among a prosperous people.

barriers.quote: a winnowing shovel
barriers.my_reading: A flat farm tool for tossing threshed grain so the wind blows the husks away. It looks like an oar, so someone mistaking the oar for one proves Odysseus has reached people who have never seen the sea.
barriers.note: Few modern readers know the tool, and the whole sign depends on it.

barriers.quote: do not even mix salt with their food
barriers.my_reading: They live so far inland that they don't know (sea) salt.

barriers.quote: sacrifice a ram, a bull, and a boar to Poseidon
barriers.my_reading: The offering is to make peace with the sea god, presumably because Poseidon is hostile to Odysseus, but Book 23 never says so or why.
barriers.note: Outside knowledge only: Poseidon's anger at Odysseus.

barriers.quote: death should come to me from the sea
barriers.my_reading: Unclear whether death comes out of the sea or far away from it. It seems to clash with the gentle death in old age described straight afterwards.
barriers.note: Outside knowledge only: the phrase in this prophecy is traditionally ambiguous.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Penelope takes comfort: if the gods will give him a happier old age, then at least there is hope of an end to his troubles.

Meanwhile Eurynome and the nurse make up the bed by torchlight with soft covers. The nurse goes off to sleep, and Eurynome, the bedroom attendant, lights Odysseus and Penelope to their room and leaves; they gladly return to their old marriage bed. Telemachus and the two herdsmen stop dancing, make the women stop too, and lie down to sleep in the hall.

barriers.quote: the nurse went back into the house
barriers.my_reading: She returned to her own quarters. 'Back into the house' suggests the bedroom is outside the house, which is confusing.

barriers.quote: the rites of their own old bed
barriers.my_reading: A delicate way of saying they made love and resumed married life in their own bed. 'Rites' suggests a religious ceremony.

barriers.quote: Telemachus, Philoetius, and the swineherd
barriers.my_reading: Odysseus's son plus two loyal servants: a swineherd (pig-keeper) and Philoetius, apparently another herdsman. Neither has been introduced in this Book; ¶28 names Eumaeus, presumably the swineherd.

paragraphs.paraphrase: After making love they talk. Penelope tells him what she endured watching the suitors crowd the house for her sake, slaughtering sheep and cattle and drinking cask after cask of wine. Odysseus tells her everything he suffered and all the trouble he caused others, and she is so enthralled that she stays awake until he has finished.

His story runs in order: victory over the Cicons; the Lotus-eaters' land; the Cyclops who ate his men, and his revenge; Aeolus, who helped him on his way, though a hurricane blew him back out to sea; the Laestrygonians of Telepylos, who destroyed all his ships but his own; Circe and her tricks; the journey to the land of the dead to consult Tiresias, where he saw old comrades and his mother; the Sirens' song; the Wandering Rocks, Charybdis and Scylla; his men eating the sun-god's cattle, for which Zeus struck the ship with lightning and left him the sole survivor; Calypso on her island, who kept him, wanted to marry him and offered him immortality, which he refused; and finally the Phaeacians, who honored him like a god and shipped him home with rich gifts. Then he falls asleep.

barriers.quote: the Cicons
barriers.my_reading: Some people he fought and defeated early on; who they are is not said.
barriers.note: The whole paragraph is a catalogue of names that assumes the earlier Books.

barriers.quote: the fertile land of the Lotus-eaters
barriers.my_reading: A people in a fertile land; why they matter is not said.
barriers.note: Outside knowledge only: their lotus made men forget home.

barriers.quote: but even so he was not to reach home, for to his great grief a hurricane carried him out to sea again
barriers.my_reading: Aeolus helped him (how is not said), but a storm drove him back out to sea anyway. The connection between the help and the storm is unexplained.
barriers.note: Outside knowledge only: Aeolus gave him the winds in a bag, which his men opened.

barriers.quote: cunning Circe and her craft
barriers.my_reading: 'Craft' = magic or trickery; Circe is apparently a sorceress.
barriers.note: 'Craft' could mean skill, a boat or witchcraft; outside knowledge only.

barriers.quote: the Wandering rocks and terrible Charybdis and to Scylla, whom no man had ever yet passed in safety
barriers.my_reading: Deadly sea hazards: moving rocks, Charybdis (a whirlpool) and Scylla (a monster). Only 'whom' hints that Scylla is a creature.
barriers.note: Outside knowledge only.

barriers.quote: his men then ate the cattle of the sun-god, and how Zeus therefore struck the ship
barriers.my_reading: The cattle were sacred and forbidden, so eating them was a sacrilege Zeus punished. 'Therefore' implies this, but the ban is never stated.

barriers.quote: the Ogygian island
barriers.my_reading: Calypso's island, evidently named Ogygia.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Athena then acts again: once she judges Odysseus has had enough love and sleep, she makes Dawn rise from the ocean. Odysseus gets up and tells Penelope that, after all they have both suffered, she should now look after the property in the house. He will replace the livestock the suitors ate, partly by raiding other people and partly by making the Greeks pay compensation. He is going to the countryside to see his grieving father, and warns her that by sunrise the killings will be public knowledge, so she should stay upstairs with her women, see no one and ask nothing.

barriers.quote: had had enough both of his wife and of rest
barriers.my_reading: Had enjoyed enough lovemaking and sleep. The modern idiom 'had enough of' (= fed up with) makes it sound as if he had tired of his wife.

barriers.quote: gold-enthroned Dawn rise out of Oceanus
barriers.my_reading: The Dawn goddess, pictured on a golden throne, rises from the ocean at the world's edge; in plain terms, the sun came up.

barriers.quote: will make the Achaeans replace the rest until they have filled all my yards
barriers.my_reading: He will force the local Greeks (his own people? the suitors' families?) to compensate him with animals until his pens are full. Who 'the Achaeans' are here is unclear, and 'yards' means animal pens.

barriers.quote: it will at once get abroad
barriers.my_reading: The news will spread at once (not 'go overseas').
barriers.note: Archaic.

paragraphs.paraphrase: As he speaks he puts on his armor and wakes Telemachus, Philoetius and Eumaeus, who arm too. They open the gates and set out with Odysseus in front; although it is already daylight, Athena hides them in darkness and leads them quickly out of town.

barriers.quote: sallied forth
barriers.my_reading: Marched out, as on an expedition.
barriers.note: Archaic.

book_level: 'Gallery' is used for the main hall (¶2, ¶8, ¶24). A modern reader pictures a balcony, a corridor or an art gallery; only the fire and pillars in ¶8 show it is the great hall.

Supporting characters are never introduced. Eurycleia is only 'the nurse', and whose nurse is never said (it reads as Penelope's). Eurynome's name sounds almost the same. Philoetius, 'the swineherd' and Eumaeus appear without introduction and without saying which is which.

Background myth is assumed rather than explained: Troy (only 'that city with its ill-omened name'), 'Achaean(s)', Helen and why she matters, Hephaestus, Oceanus and Dawn's horses, Tiresias and Hades, and why Poseidon needs appeasing.

The register drifts from easy modern English (¶0–7) to noticeably archaic English from ¶10 on: 'tokens with which we two are alone acquainted', 'Look to it yourself', 'presently', 'I would have you consider', 'take it amiss', 'deemed', 'bade', 'get abroad', 'sallied forth'.

Penelope's reasoning is hard to follow: tears of joy (¶3) then flat denial (¶5), the 'counsels of the gods' reply (¶7), the ambiguous 'I am not struck by your appearance' (¶16), and a bed order that is revealed as a test only afterwards ('She said this to try him').

Physical descriptions are hard to picture on a phone: the seating geometry in ¶8, 'this room' versus 'the bedroom' in ¶16, and the carpentry of the bed built around the olive trunk in ¶17 (the key fact, that the bed is rooted to a living tree, survives, but the details don't).

Long similes with inserted clauses (gilded silver in ¶15, shipwreck survivors in ¶19, where the viewpoint switches from him to her) and the one-paragraph adventure catalogue in ¶26 are hard to follow aloud; ¶26 is a list of unexplained names for anyone who doesn't already know the story.
Odysseus repeats Telemachus's rebuke from ¶9 word for word in ¶15. It reads either as an intentional echo or as an editing slip.
